C1.rationale: Level 2 anchor is satisfied: assessed collaborative practice recurs systematically across finance and management core subjects with individual exam accountability and group presentations. In ACCT90004 Accounting for Decision Making, students complete a 3000-word group assignment in teams of 3–4; in ECOM90009 Quantitative Methods, students complete multiple group assignments and group oral presentations; in FNCE90060 Financial Management, students submit group homework problem sets; and in FNCE90062 Capstone Studies in Finance, teams of 5–6 students deliver a 5000-word final valuation assignment and oral presentation. Level 3 is not met: while teams use financial spreadsheets and terminals, formal assessed role-and-tool allocation charters dividing work between human financial analysts and autonomous AI investment/valuation agents are unevidenced.

C2.rationale: Level 2 anchor is satisfied: core assessment includes criterion-referenced appraisal of financial assets, derivative valuation, corporate capital structure decisions, and investment performance in complex market case studies. In FNCE90011 Derivative Securities, students evaluate option pricing bounds and hedging strategies; in FNCE90018 Corporate Financial Policy, students appraise M&A financing and payout policies; in FNCE90056 Investment Management, students evaluate portfolio performance against benchmarks; and in FNCE90062 Capstone, students critically evaluate corporate valuation models. Level 3 is not met: no core assessment requires students to document and justify reliance decisions regarding AI-driven financial analysis, algorithmic trading signals, or automated portfolio optimization tools with systematic override logs over time.

C3.rationale: Level 2 anchor is satisfied: core units directly address quantitative financial modeling, statistical reasoning, algorithmic asset pricing, and financial computer software. In ECOM90009 Quantitative Methods for Business, students complete quantitative econometric modeling; in FNCE90056 Investment Management, students apply statistical tools and portfolio analytics; and the course attributes emphasize adeptness in using financial computer software. Level 3 is not met: systemic critique of AI governance in financial markets (algorithmic market manipulation, algorithmic bias in credit risk modeling, systemic liquidity risks of autonomous trading agents, APRA/ASIC AI compliance) is not formally assessed in the core.
